turns.prompt_text: I have two mindstorm NXT devices. I know one of them works and I just bought some cheap AA batteries for it but I can't get it to turn on
turns.response_html:
It can be incredibly frustrating when you know a piece of hardware works, but it suddenly refuses to cooperate over something as simple as fresh batteries.

With the Lego Mindstorms NXT intelligent brick, there are a few hardware quirks that commonly cause this exact issue. Because you mentioned using "cheap" AA batteries, there is a very specific physical culprit we should look at first.

1. Check for Terminal Contact (The "Cheap Battery" Issue)

This is the most common reason an NXT brick won't turn on with certain battery brands.

The NXT battery compartment is designed with strict tolerances. Many inexpensive or generic AA batteries have a positive terminal nub (the "+" button tip) that is slightly shorter or wider than name-brand alternatives like Duracell or Energizer.

Because of the plastic molding inside the NXT's battery tray, a shorter nub won't physically reach the metal contact plate. The battery looks like it's seated perfectly, but no current flows.

  • The Fix: Take a close look at the positive terminals inside the tray. If the metal tabs are slightly bent backward, you can use a small flathead screwdriver or a paperclip to gently pry them forward just a fraction of a millimeter to ensure they make solid contact with the battery tips.

2. Look for Spring Tension and Corrosion

Since these devices have likely been sitting in storage for a while, the negative terminal springs can lose their tension or suffer from minor oxidation.

  • Check the Springs: Ensure the springs on the negative side are fully extended and pushing the batteries firmly forward against the positive contacts.
  • Check for Leftover Residue: Even if you don't see bright blue or white crusty acid, a thin, clear film of oxidation can build up on the contacts over the years. Rubbing the metal contact points firmly with a pencil eraser or a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol can clean it right up.

3. The "Clicking" Firmware Crash (The Brick is Stuck)

If the physical battery contacts are completely fine but the screen stays dead, the NXT's firmware might be locked up.

Listen incredibly closely to the brick when the batteries are in. Do you hear a very faint, repetitive click-click-click sound coming from the internal speaker?

If you do, the brick is actually powered on but its firmware is corrupted or stuck in a boot loop.

  • The Reset Fix: There is a tiny, hidden reset button located on the back of the NXT brick. It is tucked inside one of the Lego Technic peg holes—specifically the one directly underneath the USB port inside the battery compartment (or near the top corner depending on the hardware revision).
  • Use a paperclip to press and hold that button down for about 5 to 10 seconds. If it was stuck, this will force it into firmware update mode (you might hear a continuous clicking or ticking), allowing you to re-flash it via a computer.

Give the USB power test a shot first to see if the brain itself wakes up, and let me know if you hear that faint ticking sound!

turns.prompt_text: One of the Duracells actually was pressed in so the positive end wasn't touching.
turns.response_html:
That is exactly what usually happens! Those little positive tabs inside the NXT tray can be surprisingly stubborn, and it only takes a fraction of a millimeter of space to break the whole circuit.

Once you get that tab gently pried back out or ensure the battery is seated firmly against it, you should hear that classic, familiar NXT startup chime when you hit the orange button.

Did adjusting that tab get it back up and running, or is it still being a bit finicky?

turns.prompt_text: I have the second NXT that still does not run, but I don't think I've ever got it to run.
turns.response_html:
Since you've never seen this second one run, it’s the perfect candidate for a quick triage to see if it's a quick fix or a dead motherboard.

Because we just solved a battery contact issue on the first one, let's bypass the battery tray completely to see if the internal board is even alive.

The 30-Second Triage

1. The USB Bypass Test (Do this first)

Take all the batteries out of the second brick and plug it directly into a computer or a USB wall adapter using a standard USB cable.

  • If it turns on or makes a sound: The internal motherboard is completely fine! This means the issue is strictly a broken connection between the battery tray and the circuit board inside.
  • If it stays completely dead: The issue is deeper down on the board itself (like a blown surface-mount fuse or a dead voltage regulator).

2. Listen for the "Click of Life"

If you put working batteries into it and press the orange button, hold the speaker right up to your ear. Do you hear a very faint, rhythmic ticking or clicking sound?

  • If you hear clicking, the brick actually is getting power, but its brain is stuck in a corrupted firmware loop. A 10-second press of the hidden reset button (inside the Lego peg hole directly under the USB port) will usually shock it back to life.

If the USB test works but batteries don't, it usually means a wire or a solder joint connecting the battery clips to the motherboard has snapped inside over the years.

Let me know what happens when you plug it into USB—that will tell us exactly which path to take!

turns.prompt_text: Okay, I'm not writing an NXT program. I'm trying to make the motor run forward for 5 seconds. Wait to run backward for 5 seconds. Wait too but it gets stuck on the first one where it jolts forward and then stops moving
turns.response_html:
If the motor is jolting forward briefly and then freezing, your NXT brick is almost certainly triggering its overcurrent protection or experiencing a voltage drop.

When an NXT motor starts up from a complete standstill, it draws a massive spike of current (amperage). If the batteries can't supply that sudden burst, the brick's internal voltage drops below the threshold required to keep the main processor running, causing it to crash and freeze instantly.

Since we just talked about cheap AA batteries and loose battery contacts on your other brick, here is exactly what is happening and how to fix it:

The Culprits

1. High Internal Resistance (The "Cheap Battery" Limit)

Inexpensive generic batteries (especially heavy-duty or cheap alkaline cells) have high internal resistance. They are fine for low-drain devices like TV remotes, but Lego NXT motors are incredibly power-hungry. When the motor asks for full power, a cheap battery's voltage instantly plummets, causing the NXT brain to lock up right as the motor starts moving.

2. A Genuinely Stiff or Binding Motor

If the gears inside that specific NXT motor have become stiff, sticky, or jammed over years of storage, the motor will experience a "stall condition." A stalling motor draws maximum current trying to force itself to turn. This will instantly trip the NXT's safety cut-off or crash the brick.

How to Troubleshoot It

Step 1: The Manual Rotation Test

Unplug the motor from the brick. Take a Lego axle or just use your fingers to turn the orange rotatable hub on the motor manually.

  • Does it turn smoothly with a consistent, clicky gear resistance?
  • Or is it completely locked up or incredibly hard to twist? If it's locked up, the internal gears are jammed, causing the electrical jolt and instant freeze.

Step 2: Test via the Built-In "View" Menu

Instead of running code, let's use the NXT's built-in firmware tools to isolate the issue:

  1. Turn on the NXT brick.
  2. Navigate to the NXT Program or Try Me menu on the screen (or use the View menu to check motor rotation).
  3. If you use the Try Me function for a motor, it runs a pre-set low-power script. If it runs fine there but crashes on your code, your batteries definitely cannot handle full-power acceleration bursts.

Step 3: Check for the "Zombie" Freeze

When it gets stuck on that first jolt, look closely at the NXT screen.

  • Is the screen still showing the active running icon, or is the screen completely frozen/blank?
  • If the screen glitches or blanks out, the cheap batteries are 100% the issue. You will need high-drain, name-brand alkalines (like Duracell/Energizer) or high-quality rechargeable NiMH batteries (like Eneloops) to drive Lego motors reliably.

Try turning the motor hub by hand first to make sure the hardware isn't physically jammed!
